scenes.transcript: Berlin 1953, a city divided
by barbed wire, ideology and
fear. On one side,
American soldiers drove through streets,
filled with rebuilding factories, bright
shop windows, and the sound
of jazz, on the other.
Soviet soldiers watched over a city where every
conversation could carry a risk, but beneath the streets,
beyond the checkpoints and guard towers,
something extraordinary was about to happen.
American and British intelligence were planning to dig
a secret tunnel under Soviet, controlled territory.
Their objective was simple, listen
to the Soviet military, every
telephone call, every teletype message,
every military conversation that passed
through three critical communication cables.
The operation was called gold, and the
CIA believed it could become one of the
greatest intelligence victories of the Cold War.
There was only one problem, the
KGB already knew, and the man
responsible was working inside British intelligence.
His name was George Blake, to
understand how this operation became possible.
We need to return to the beginning. In
1953, the Cold War was entering a dangerous phase.
The United States and the
Soviet Union were competing for military
advantage, political influence, and intelligence.
Germany had become the center of that struggle.
The country was divided into occupation zones.
With Berlin itself divided between Western
and Soviet control, West Berlin
was an island of Western
influence surrounded by communist, controlled territory.
For American intelligence, the Soviet
military presence in East Germany
represented a major uncertainty, how many
troops were ready to move,
were military exercises routine, was Moscow
preparing for a confrontation with
the West, the CIA needed answers,
but collecting them was difficult. Five
planes had serious limitations. Human sources
inside Soviet military structures were rare.
Radio intelligence could reveal some activity,
but it could not provide everything.
Then came a possible solution. A
tunnel. The British had already tested the
concept in Vienna during Operation Silver.
British intelligence had secretly
accessed Soviet communication cables
through an underground tunnel.
The operation demonstrated that underground cable
tapping could produce valuable intelligence.
Now the Americans wanted to take that
idea further. A much larger operation, a
more dangerous location, and a target directly connected
to Soviet military communications in East Berlin.
The CIA and Britain's MI6 joined
forces. The Americans would provide much
of the funding and operational support.
The British would contribute their experience
in underground construction and cable interception.
Together, they developed Operation Gold. The plan
was extraordinary. Engineers would construct a
tunnel from the American sector of Berlin.
Passing beneath the border into
Soviet, controlled territory. At the
far end, they would reach
underground communication cables, once connected.
Listening equipment would capture conversations and teletype
traffic. The intelligence would then be
recorded, processed, and sent back for analysis.
But there was a major challenge.
The tunnel had to remain completely
hidden. The operation required careful engineering, strict
compartmentalization, and a convincing cover story.
A warehouse would conceal the
entrance. Construction activity would appear
ordinary. Workers and engineers would
operate under layers of secrecy.
Even the removal of excavated soil
required planning. Every detail mattered.
